forms.definition: the title a university gives you after you finish your studies
forms.example: She has a degree in economics from Tashkent State University.
forms.note: degree also means a unit for measuring temperature or angles (20 degrees).

syn.note: Any official proof that you finished a course; wider than a university title.
The paper you get; in some countries also a shorter course.
An official paper that shows you passed something.

context.text: My cousin finished her degree last summer. Now she wants to work as an engineer in Samarkand.

reviewer_note: Temperature/angle meaning noted only; no family forms exist.

forms.definition: a time when you must wait longer than planned
forms.example: There was a two-hour delay at the airport.

syn.note: Moving an event to a later time; more formal.
The time you spend waiting for something.

forms.definition: to make something happen later than planned
forms.example: Snow delayed our train by an hour.

syn.note: To move an event to a later time on purpose.
A formal word for postpone.
To make something go less fast.

forms.definition: arriving or happening later than planned
forms.example: Our delayed flight finally left at midnight.

syn.note: The easiest word: not on time.
Later than it should be, often for payments or books.

context.text: Heavy snow delayed all the buses this morning. Because of the long delay, I was late for my first lesson.

reviewer_note: Noun/verb conversion pair; delayed as participial adjective.

forms.definition: bringing goods or letters to a person or place
forms.example: The shop offers free delivery in the city.

syn.note: Goods sent together, often by a company.
Giving things out to many people or places.

forms.definition: to take goods or letters to the right address
forms.example: The post office delivers letters every morning.

syn.note: To come with something to a place; the easiest word.
To hold something while you move it.
To make something go to a place; you do not take it yourself.

ant.note: To go and get something from a place.

context.text: The bakery delivers fresh bread to our street every day. The delivery always comes before seven o'clock.

reviewer_note: deliver = give birth / give a speech not shown; deliverable (business noun) left out as rare for learners.

forms.definition: the act of bringing things to a person or place
forms.example: We are waiting for a delivery of new chairs.

syn.note: Goods sent together, often by a company.
Giving things out to many people or places.

forms.definition: to take goods or letters to the right address
forms.example: Can you deliver the sofa on Saturday?
forms.note: The headword is made from this verb: deliver + -y.

syn.note: To come with something to a place; the easiest word.
To hold something while you move it.

ant.note: To go and get something from a place.

context.text: My order from the online shop arrived this morning. The driver delivered it to my door, and the delivery was free.

reviewer_note: Same family as deliver; separate map for the noun headword.

forms.definition: one part of a big company, shop, school or government
forms.example: My uncle works in the sales department.

syn.note: One part of something bigger.
A large part of a company; often bigger than a department.
A room or group of people who do one kind of work.

forms.note: depart (= leave) shares an old root but has a different meaning today.

forms.definition: belonging to one part of a company or school
forms.example: We have a departmental meeting every Monday.

context.text: My sister works in the history department of a big school. Every Friday she goes to a departmental meeting with the other teachers.

reviewer_note: department store is a compound and left out (Rule 7); depart as not_family.

forms.definition: the act of leaving a place to start a journey
forms.example: Please arrive one hour before departure.

syn.note: Leaving a room or building.
The moment a plane leaves the ground.

ant.note: The act of reaching a place.

forms.definition: to leave a place, especially to start a trip
forms.example: The train departs from platform two.

syn.note: The easiest everyday word.
To move away from a place.

forms.definition: leaving a place soon or now
forms.example: The screen shows all departing flights.

syn.note: Going out or away.

context.text: Our departure from Tashkent was at six in the morning. The plane departed late because of fog.

reviewer_note: 2 rows merged (same meaning, B1). depart marked formal.

forms.definition: a movement from a higher place to a lower one
forms.example: The plane began its descent into Bukhara.

syn.note: A fall to a lower level.
Going down quickly, often by accident.

forms.note: descent also means your family origin (of Uzbek descent).

forms.definition: to move from a higher place to a lower place
forms.example: We descended the mountain before dark.

syn.note: To go down to a lower level.
To go down quickly, often by accident.

forms.definition: going down from higher to lower
forms.example: Write the numbers in descending order.

syn.note: Going down.

people.definition: a person who comes from an older member of the same family
people.example: He is a descendant of Amir Temur.
people.note: Belongs to descend = come from a family line, not going down.

context.text: The hikers descended the mountain slowly. The descent took three hours, but the view was beautiful.

reviewer_note: Everyday go down / climb down are phrasal; easy synonyms limited. descendant kept as other_meaning person.

forms.definition: the way something looks or is planned
forms.example: I like the simple design of this phone.

syn.note: The way something looks.
How the parts of a page, room or place are arranged.
Lines or shapes repeated as decoration.

forms.definition: to plan how something will look and work
forms.example: She designs clothes for a shop in Tashkent.

syn.note: To decide in detail how to do or make something.
To make something new.
To make a picture with a pen or pencil.

forms.definition: planned and made for a special use
forms.example: This bag is designed for long trips.

syn.note: Decided or arranged before.

people.definition: a person whose job is to plan how things look

context.text: I really like the design of my new phone. It was designed by a small team in Korea.

reviewer_note: Headword marked (n) in corpus; noun is the base. designate/designation not family in meaning.

forms.definition: the place someone or something is going to
forms.example: Samarkand is a popular destination for tourists.

syn.note: The last stop of a bus or train line.
A place where a bus or train stops.
Something you want to reach; often not a place.

forms.definition: certain to happen because of fate
forms.example: She felt she was destined to be a doctor.
forms.note: Belongs to destine = decide someone's future, not a place you travel to.

context.text: After a long train ride, we finally reached our destination. Khiva was even more beautiful than we expected.

reviewer_note: destined (fate) kept as other_meaning; destiny not shown (rare link for learners).

forms.definition: very great damage that leaves nothing useful
forms.example: The storm caused terrible destruction.

syn.note: Harm to something; it may still be usable.
The state of being badly broken.

forms.definition: to damage something so badly that it cannot be used
forms.example: The fire destroyed the old school.

syn.note: To damage something completely.
To break a car, ship or building badly.
To knock down a building on purpose.
To make something go into pieces; the easiest word.

ant.note: To make a building or thing.

forms.definition: causing a lot of damage
forms.example: Floods can be very destructive.

syn.note: Causing harm.
Bad for people or things.

forms.definition: in a way that causes damage
forms.example: The angry child behaved destructively.

syn.note: In a way that hurts.

people.definition: a small, fast ship used in war
people.example: A navy destroyer sailed past the port.

context.text: Last year a big fire destroyed a market in our town. The destruction was terrible, but people rebuilt it quickly.

reviewer_note: destructive/destruction from Latin destruct-; -ive not marked as an affix (destruct is not an everyday word).
